overview.what_it_is: A ratio compares amounts using the same-sized parts.

format_facts.label: Main skill
format_facts.value: Compare two or three amounts using ratios.

format_facts.label: Ratio sign
format_facts.value: Use a colon between each number.

format_facts.label: Reading
format_facts.value: Read the colon as the word "to".

format_facts.label: Order
format_facts.value: Write amounts in the order named.

format_facts.label: Study time
format_facts.value: About three hours with short practice breaks.

scoring_factors.name: Correct order
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each number matches the named amount.

scoring_factors.name: Equal changes
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether every ratio part changes by the same factor.

scoring_factors.name: Correct working
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each unit step is clearly shown.

scoring_factors.name: Clear answer
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the answer includes the correct unit.

critical_rules: The first number matches the first amount named.
The larger amount does not always come first.
Multiply every ratio part by the same number.
Divide every ratio part by the same number.
Use a common factor for all three parts.
Add ratio parts before sharing a total.

learning_goals: You will read a ratio using the word "to".
You will write ratios in the correct order.
You will reverse a ratio without changing its meaning.
You will find ratios that show the same comparison.
You will write ratios in their simplest form.
You will find missing amounts using unit parts.
You will compare three amounts with one ratio.

core_method.name: Name → Match → Make Units → Find
core_method.summary: Name each amount. Match the parts. Find one unit.

steps.detail: Underline the amounts in the order given.
Match each amount to its ratio number.
Make sure the first amount comes first.
Count the ratio parts linked to the known amount.
Divide the known amount by its unit count.
Multiply one unit by the needed units.
Check the size, order, and measurement unit.

core_method.formula: Known amount $\div$ known units $=$ one unit; one unit $\times$ needed units $=$ answer.

techniques.name: Keep the named order
techniques.purpose: Stops the two ratio numbers being reversed.
how_to: Read the two amounts from left to right.
Write the first amount above the first number.
Write the second amount above the second number.
Check both labels before doing any working.
techniques.example: For white to red, $1 : 3$ means one white part and three red parts.
techniques.why_it_matters: A reversed ratio answers a different question.
techniques.common_error: Writing the bigger number first without checking names.

techniques.name: Reverse both parts
techniques.purpose: Finds the ratio in the opposite order.
how_to: Read the new order in the question.
Swap the first and second ratio numbers.
Do not add or subtract the numbers.
Read the new ratio aloud to check.
techniques.example: If cats to dogs is $2 : 5$, dogs to cats is $5 : 2$.
techniques.why_it_matters: The comparison changes when the order changes.
techniques.common_error: Keeping $2 : 5$ after the names are reversed.

techniques.name: Make the same ratio
techniques.purpose: Creates ratios with the same relationship.
how_to: Choose one whole-number factor.
Multiply every part by that factor.
Or divide every part by that factor.
Check that all parts changed equally.
techniques.why_it_matters: The amounts grow, but their comparison stays unchanged.
techniques.common_error: Changing only one number in the ratio.

techniques.name: Reach the simplest form
techniques.purpose: Writes the ratio using the smallest whole numbers.
how_to: List factors shared by every ratio number.
Choose the greatest common factor.
Divide every number by that factor.
Check that no larger common factor remains.
techniques.why_it_matters: Small numbers make the relationship easier to see.
techniques.common_error: Dividing each part by a different number.

techniques.name: Find one unit
techniques.purpose: Finds a missing amount from a known amount.
how_to: Match the known amount to its ratio units.
Divide the amount by those units.
This gives the value of one unit.
Multiply by the units you need.
techniques.example: If $7$ units equal $21$ m, then $1$ unit equals $21 \div 7 = 3$ m.
techniques.why_it_matters: One unit links the ratio to real measurements.

techniques.name: Share a total
techniques.purpose: Splits one total using two or three ratio parts.
how_to: Add all ratio numbers first.
The sum is the total unit count.
Divide the total by that count.
Multiply by the required ratio part.
techniques.why_it_matters: The total belongs to all ratio parts together.
techniques.common_error: Dividing the total by only one ratio number.

worked_examples.title: Write a ratio in simplest form
worked_examples.decoding: Both numbers count birds. Find their greatest common factor.
worked_examples.plan: Divide both numbers by the same greatest factor.
worked_examples.model_answer: The common factors include $1$ and $3$. The greatest common factor is $3$. Divide both parts by $3$. $15 \div 3 = 5$. $12 \div 3 = 4$. Therefore, $15 : 12 = 5 : 4$. The simplest ratio is $5 : 4$.

annotations.comment: Using the largest factor finishes in one step.
The first ratio part is divided by $3$.
The second part uses the same divisor.
The two numbers share no larger common factor.

worked_examples.title: Find boys to girls
worked_examples.input: There are $40$ students. There are $25$ boys. Write boys to girls in simplest form.
worked_examples.decoding: The number of girls is not given directly.
worked_examples.plan: Find the girls first. Then write and reduce the ratio.
worked_examples.model_answer: First find the number of girls. $40 - 25 = 15$. There are $15$ girls. Boys to girls is $25 : 15$. Both numbers share a factor of $5$. $25 \div 5 = 5$. $15 \div 5 = 3$. Therefore, $25 : 15 = 5 : 3$. The ratio of boys to girls is $5 : 3$.

annotations.comment: Subtract boys from all students to find girls.
Boys come first because boys are named first.
Both ratio parts must use the same divisor.
This is the ratio in its simplest form.

worked_examples.title: Find a missing ribbon length
worked_examples.input: Ribbon A is $21$ m long. The ratio of A to B is $7 : 4$. Find Ribbon B.
worked_examples.decoding: Ribbon A matches $7$ units. Ribbon B matches $4$ units.
worked_examples.plan: Find one unit from Ribbon A. Then find four units.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: Ribbon A has $7$ equal parts. Ribbon B has $4$ equal parts. Ribbon A measures $21$ m. Find one part. $21 \div 7 = 3$ m. Ribbon B has $4$ parts. $4 \times 3 = 12$ m. Ribbon B is $12$ m long.

annotations.comment: The equal parts show what each ratio number means.
This finds the length of one equal part.
Ribbon B contains four equal parts.
The final answer includes the correct length unit.

worked_examples.title: Share money using a ratio
worked_examples.input: Siti and Mary share $\$35$ in the ratio $4 : 3$. How much does Siti receive?
worked_examples.decoding: The whole amount covers both shares together.
worked_examples.plan: Add the units. Find one unit. Then find Siti's share.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: Siti has $4$ equal parts. Mary has $3$ equal parts. Together, they have $4 + 3 = 7$ parts. The total is $\$35$. One part is $\$35 \div 7 = \$5$. Siti has $4$ parts. Her share is $4 \times \$5 = \$20$. Siti receives $\$20$.

annotations.comment: All ratio parts make the complete money amount.
Dividing finds the value of one part.
Siti receives four equal parts.
The answer uses the money sign.

worked_examples.title: Find a rectangle width
worked_examples.input: Length to width is $3 : 4$. The length is $12$ cm. Find the width.
worked_examples.decoding: The length matches $3$ units. The width matches $4$ units.
worked_examples.plan: Use the length to find one unit. Then find four units.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: The length has $3$ equal parts. The width has $4$ equal parts. The length is $12$ cm. One part is $12 \div 3 = 4$ cm. The width has $4$ parts. $4 \times 4 = 16$ cm. The rectangle is $16$ cm wide.

annotations.comment: The first number matches the rectangle's length.
This gives the size of one equal part.
The width uses four equal parts.
The answer is larger because four parts exceed three.

worked_examples.title: Split water into three buckets
worked_examples.input: $20$ L of water is shared in the ratio $2 : 3 : 5$. Find bucket C.
worked_examples.decoding: Bucket C is the third amount. It matches $5$ units.
worked_examples.plan: Add all units. Find one unit. Then find five units.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: Bucket A has $2$ parts. Bucket B has $3$ parts. Bucket C has $5$ parts. Total units are $2 + 3 + 5 = 10$. One unit is $20 \div 10 = 2$ L. Bucket C has $5$ units. $5 \times 2 = 10$ L. Bucket C contains $10$ L.

annotations.comment: All three parts belong to the total volume.
This finds the volume in one ratio unit.
Bucket C matches the third ratio number.
The result is half of the total water.

worked_examples.title: Correct a reversed ratio
worked_examples.input: There are $24$ female teachers and $10$ male teachers. Mia writes male to female as $24 : 10$. Correct her answer.
worked_examples.decoding: Male teachers are named first. Their number must come first.
worked_examples.plan: Correct the order. Then write the simplest form.
worked_examples.model_answer: Mia reversed the two amounts. There are $10$ male teachers and $24$ female teachers. Male to female is $10 : 24$. Both numbers share a factor of $2$. $10 \div 2 = 5$. $24 \div 2 = 12$. Therefore, $10 : 24 = 5 : 12$. The correct simplest ratio is $5 : 12$.

annotations.comment: Male comes first because male is named first.
The first part is reduced using $2$.
The second part uses the same divisor.
The ratio now has correct order and form.

worked_examples.title: Find the total package weight
worked_examples.input: Package X to Package Y is $5 : 3$. Package X weighs $40$ kg. Find their total weight.
worked_examples.decoding: Package X matches $5$ units. Both packages use $8$ units.
worked_examples.plan: Find one unit. Then multiply by all eight units.
worked_examples.model_answer: Bar model: Package X has $5$ parts. Package Y has $3$ parts. Package X weighs $40$ kg. One part is $40 \div 5 = 8$ kg. Both packages have $5 + 3 = 8$ parts. Their total weight is $8 \times 8 = 64$ kg. Both packages weigh $64$ kg altogether.

annotations.comment: This finds the weight of one ratio part.
The total includes both packages.
Eight parts each weigh eight kilograms.
The answer states the total weight clearly.

items.when_to_use: Use it when comparing two or more amounts.
Say this word when reading the colon.
Use it for one number in a ratio.
Use it when comparing three different amounts.
Match it to the first ratio number.
Match it to the second ratio number.
Match it to the third ratio number.
Use it when the named order changes.
Use it for ratios showing the same relationship.
Use it when changing every ratio part.
Use it for a number dividing every part.
Use it when no larger common factor remains.
Use it for one equal part of a ratio.
Use it for the amount already given.
Use it for the amount you must find.
Use it after adding all ratio numbers.
Use it when the question measures length.
Use it when the question measures weight.
Use it when the question measures volume.
Use it when the question involves money.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Ratio order follows names, not number size.
common_mistakes.fix: Underline the amounts and keep their named order.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The answer then compares the amounts backwards.
common_mistakes.fix: Label each ratio number before writing the answer.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The new ratio no longer shows the same relationship.
common_mistakes.fix: Multiply or divide every part by one factor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using different divisors for each part.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The ratio changes into a different comparison.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose one common factor for every ratio number.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The ratio still uses larger numbers than needed.
common_mistakes.fix: Check whether all parts share another common factor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the total as one ratio part.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The total often covers all parts together.
common_mistakes.fix: Add the ratio numbers before dividing the total.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The real value of each equal part stays unknown.
common_mistakes.fix: Divide the known amount by its ratio units first.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The number alone does not fully answer the question.
common_mistakes.fix: Write metres, litres, kilograms, or dollars.

time_budget.focus: Recall factors and basic division facts.
Read ratios and match each named amount.
Multiply and divide every part equally.
Use common factors to reduce ratios.
Find one unit before missing amounts.
Add units and split a total.
Solve mixed questions and explain each answer.

drills.name: Name and match
drills.instructions: Label both amounts in ten short ratio questions.

drills.name: Reverse it
drills.instructions: Write the reverse of eight given ratios.

drills.name: Build same ratios
drills.instructions: Make three matching ratios from each starting ratio.

drills.name: Factor hunt
drills.instructions: Find the greatest common factor for ten number pairs.

drills.name: Simplest form sprint
drills.instructions: Reduce ten ratios and check each common factor.

drills.name: One-unit practice
drills.instructions: Find one unit in six short word problems.

drills.name: Bar model words
drills.instructions: Describe ratio bars before doing any arithmetic.

drills.name: Three-part sharing
drills.instructions: Split five totals using three-part ratios.

practice_plan.routine: Read the question twice. Label the ratio. Draw equal parts. Show each step. Check the order and unit.

mastery_checklist: I can read the colon as "to".
I can match each number to its amount.
I can write a ratio in the named order.
I can reverse a ratio correctly.
I can make ratios with the same value.
I can write a ratio in simplest form.
I can find the value of one unit.
I can use units to find missing amounts.
I can share a total using ratio parts.
I can compare three amounts with one ratio.
I can include the correct measurement unit.
strategy_notes: Circle words showing the order of the amounts.
Write small labels above each ratio number.
Estimate whether the missing amount should be larger.
Draw a bar when the words feel confusing.
Use the greatest common factor when you know it.
Check that every ratio part changed equally.
For totals, add all ratio parts before dividing.
Read your final answer as a full sentence.
